analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to refund baggage fees when bags are lost, delayed, or damaged, and to disclose fees upfront.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a House floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required airlines to give passengers their baggage fees back — within 30 days — whenever a checked bag is lost, damaged, or delayed more than an hour after landing. It would also have required airlines and ticket agents, before selling a ticket, to ask whether a passenger has bags to check and tell them what each checked bag costs. The bill went to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and was sent to its Aviation subcommittee, where no further action was taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers who check bags. Today an airline can charge $25 or more per bag and keep that fee even if the bag never shows up on the carousel. The bill would have forced a refund of the fee whenever a bag is lost, damaged, or delayed past one hour, and forced the airline to tell you the baggage cost before you buy the ticket instead of springing it at checkout.

how_it_helps.text: Airlines must refund any baggage fee within 30 days after a flight on which a bag is lost, delayed, or damaged [S2][S3].
'Delayed' is defined concretely: a bag counts as delayed if it is not on the conveyor belt or available for pickup one hour after the flight lands at the passenger's final destination [S3].

Before selling a ticket — online, by phone, or otherwise — airlines, foreign carriers, and ticket agents must ask if the buyer has bags to check and disclose the cost of checking each one; failing to do so would be an unfair or deceptive practice under federal aviation law [S2][S3].

For online sales, the seller could satisfy this by letting the buyer indicate the number of bags while selecting flights, so the fee appears in the quoted price rather than as a surprise at the end of checkout [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Airlines and ticket agents. Airlines would refund fees on mishandled bags and lose some of the revenue from a fee they currently keep no matter what happens to the bag. Ticket agents and booking sites would have to change their sales flow to ask about bags and show the fee before completing a sale.

drawbacks.text: The one-hour trigger is strict: a bag that arrives 90 minutes late on the carousel — a common occurrence on connecting flights — would entitle the passenger to a full fee refund, a cost airlines and some fare defenders would call disproportionate to the inconvenience [S3].

Disclosure rules add compliance work for airlines, ticket agents, and online booking sites, and some of that cost is likely passed into fares; passengers who never check bags would pay for protections they don't use.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is modest per passenger but broad: virtually every flyer checks a bag eventually, and a lost or badly delayed bag is already a real cost on top of a fee the airline keeps either way. The refund requirement is simple to administer and the disclosure rule just moves existing fees into the quoted price. The main honest objection is the one-hour delay trigger, which is stricter than most travelers would demand. On balance the benefits to travelers outweigh the compliance costs, but the stakes are moderate, not transformative.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Aviation subcommittee, and it died there — no markup, no vote, and the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Capuano introduced the Baggage Fee Fairness Act of 2011 on February 15, 2011 [S1][S5].
Thirteen other House members joined as original cosponsors [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure on the day it was introduced [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Aviation, which took no further action on it [S5].
The bill received no committee vote, no floor vote, and never became law; 15 members cosponsored, all Democrats [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines kept a baggage-fee revenue stream they would otherwise have had to refund when bags went missing, and passengers continued to pay fees with no guaranteed refund when a bag is lost or delayed.

for.name: Rep. Michael Capuano
for.role: Sponsor, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require baggage-fee refunds and upfront fee disclosure.

for.name: 14 House Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors (Mrs. Christensen, Mr. Cohen, Mr. DeFazio, Mr. Jackson of Illinois, Mr. McGovern, Ms. Moore, Mr. Nadler, Ms. Norton, Ms. Richardson, Mr. Sablan, Mr. Shuler, Mr. Costello, and others)

for.name: 15 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors by the end of the session
for.what_they_did: All 15 cosponsors of the bill were Democrats; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair John Mica, R-FL)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 15, 2011 and sent it to the Aviation subcommittee; never held a markup or reported the bill.

against.name: Major U.S. airlines and their trade association
against.role: Industry affected by the fee-refund mandate
against.what_they_did: Airlines had recently imposed baggage fees as a major new revenue stream and opposed mandates that would limit or claw back those fees; no lobbying on this bill appears in the congressional record itself.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; the committee of referral was chaired by a Republican, and the bill never advanced past subcommittee referral.

industries.note: Baggage fees are a multibillion-dollar revenue stream airlines collect on top of fares; the bill would have forced refunds whenever a bag is lost, damaged, or delayed over an hour, converting an unconditional fee into a conditional one. Requiring fee disclosure before ticket sale would also expose the fee earlier in the purchase, when it can influence choices.

industries.industry: Ticket agents and online travel booking sites
industries.note: Agents and booking sites would have to redesign checkout to ask about checked bags and show the per-bag fee before a sale, an added compliance burden and, arguably, a loss of upsell revenue at the point of sale.
